On-device recognition · 1 echo line ignored

Suggested answer

2/2

So when the database and the cache both change, how do you keep them consistent?

We write to the database first, then delete the cache entry, and a binlog subscriber backs that up. It's eventually consistent.

  • After a successful write we delete the key; a read that misses goes to the database and refills the cache.
  • If the delete fails, the key goes to a retry queue, and the binlog subscriber deletes it again.
  • Hot keys get a delayed double delete, so a stale value has almost no time to sneak back in.
  • Where we need strong consistency, like balances, we read from the database or take a distributed lock.

Notes only: no automatic answers. Press ⇧⌘↩ when you need help, or type a question below.

Based on: Materials 2

In one line

The project story was solid and backed by numbers. On system design you got to the point too slowly, and the cache-breakdown answer was still incomplete.

Question by question
  1. 1

    What if deleting the cache fails? [18:22] Good

    My answer: Retry queue plus an async delete from the binlog. Two safety nets.

  2. 2

    A hot key expires and a flood of requests hits the database at once. What do you do? [27:05] To improve

    My answer: Add a lock… (8-second pause) …maybe a Bloom filter.

    Better answer

    Answer first: a mutex rebuild or logical expiry, chosen by how fresh the data must be. A Bloom filter stops penetration, not breakdown; keep them apart.

What I didn't mention

One meeting, from preparation to notes

2:02 PMHome

Home asks one thing: is there a meeting?

New meeting takes you to the prepare page. No time? Record now (⇧⌘N) skips all of that: no type, no materials, and you still get notes when it ends.

2:03 PMPrepare · 1 of 4

Say what kind of meeting it is

Eight types sit in one row. Pick one and the rest follows: prompting or notes only, how long answers run, which notes template it uses. The title says “round 2”, so Interview is already picked.

2:04 PMPrepare · 2 of 4

Round two remembers round one

It recognizes the second meeting of the same series and ticks what round one left behind: materials, the review, the lessons. The full transcript is long, so it stays unticked. Untick something and watch what the AI takes away change.

2:06 PMPrepare · 3–4 of 4

Drop files in. It reads while you get ready.

Each file goes from Reading to Read, then it writes down what it took away. Before you start there are three rows: the audio meters are moving, the answer engine is connected, the phone is paired. Three green dots and you can begin.

2:30 PMLive

During the call, the window holds this conversation and nothing else

The sidebar folds away. The transcript runs on the left; the suggested answer fades in on the right, word by word. Below it, three rewrites: Shorter, Example, In English. The rest sit behind “…”. Answer now is the only primary button in the window.

2:52 PMLive

It can stay quiet until someone asks you

Switch the top bar to Notes only and it stops answering on its own; press ⇧⌘↩ when you need it. Click the model name for Answer settings: model, fast mode, web search, length. Changes apply from the next answer.

3:14 PMEnded

End the call, and the same page becomes the notes

The transcript goes to a separate notes model. It proofreads, organizes by the interview review template, then checks each line against what was said. Questions you fumbled go into the question bank and come back when you prepare for round three.

During · Audio

It doesn’t need to know
which meeting app you use

On a call, it listens to everything your Mac plays, plus your microphone: them on one channel, you on the other. When everyone is in the same room, it uses the microphone alone and labels the transcript “Room”.

After · Notes

After the call,
notes you can send as they are

Live answers are about speed. Notes can take their time, so they get a separate model and their own process. They’re written in the background once you end, usually within one to three minutes, and you can start your next meeting meanwhile.

  1. 01

    Proofread

    Fixes recognition errors using the context and the names and terms in your materials. Nothing is re-transcribed. Every change is underlined, the original stays, and you can undo it.

    “we moved the hot queries to Redis”

  2. 02

    Organize by template

    An interview, a lab meeting and a weekly sync each get their own structure. Every item carries the moment it was said; click it to jump back to the transcript.

    Run regression tests and report results [05:40]

  3. 03

    Check

    Items with nothing behind them in the transcript are dropped. “Due Thursday” becomes a date, counted from the meeting day. Unclear names and deadlines given two ways are marked “To confirm”.

    Thursday → Thu 29 Oct To confirm

Three meetings, three kinds of notes

Every template has a section for the gaps: weak answers, questions left unsettled, risks nobody owns. That’s exactly what an ordinary summary tends to leave out.

Seven built in: interview review, academic, work meeting, client call, lecture / class, group discussion and general. Copy any of them to make your own.

During · Where to look

Answers go where
your eyes already are

The teleprompter is a slim floating strip. Drag it just below the camera and you can read without looking away. Or turn on the phone companion: scan a code to pair, and answers show up on your phone, with Shorter, Example and Previous right there.

To be clear

If you share a single window or browser tab, the teleprompter isn’t in the picture. If you share the whole screen, macOS offers no public way to guarantee it stays out; run the screen-sharing visibility test in Settings → Teleprompter, or use your phone. A phone that is shared or mirrored to the Mac can be seen too.

Where your data goes

What stays on your Mac,
and what leaves it, for whom

Stays on this Mac

Audio
Transcribed on the Mac. Recordings are never kept.
Materials
Parsed on the Mac and stored with their series.
Meetings and notes
Kept in one folder on the Mac, without audio. You can turn recording off, export or delete them.
API keys
Stored in the system keychain.

Leaves the Mac

Your answer engine
The transcript, detected questions, relevant snippets from your materials, screenshots and any skills you enabled. Codex, or an API you set up yourself.
Your notes model
This meeting’s transcript and material snippets, to write the notes. Turn automatic notes off in Settings → Notes.
Web search (when on)
Questions that need fresh information go to Codex web search, or only the question text goes to Tavily.
Cloud recognition (only if you choose it)
Once you opt in, audio streams to the provider you picked. Off by default.
Update checks
Asks GitHub whether there’s a new version.

Follow the rules of whatever meeting, class, exam or interview you’re in, and get people’s consent before recording or transcribing.

Download for Mac

GitHub Releases · InterviewHacker-version-macOS-arm64.dmg

  • The new interface, from v2.0.0
  • macOS 14 or later
  • Apple Silicon (M-series)

The repository is private for now; downloading needs access to it.

  1. 1

    Drag it into Applications

    Open the dmg and drag InterviewHacker into Applications.

  2. 2

    Open it the first time

    The app isn’t notarized by Apple yet, so macOS blocks it. Go to System Settings → Privacy & Security and click “Open Anyway” near the bottom. Or run this in Terminal:

    xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/InterviewHacker.app

  3. 3

    Click Start once

    That’s when it asks for two permissions: screen and system audio recording (to hear them) and the microphone (to hear you). The on-device speech model downloads once, about 270 MB.

  4. 4

    Connect an answer engine

    With a ChatGPT account you can use Codex. Otherwise, add an API key for any OpenAI-compatible service, such as DeepSeek, Qwen or Kimi, or point it at Ollama on your own machine.

FAQ

Questions people ask

Will the other side know I’m using it?

It doesn’t send anything into the meeting; it listens on your Mac and shows things on your screen or phone. It isn’t invisible, though: if you share your whole screen, the teleprompter may show up (see “Where to look” above). Whether and how you use it is up to the rules of the meeting.

Which meeting apps does it work with?

It doesn’t care. On a call it listens to what your Mac plays, so Zoom, Teams, Google Meet, Webex or a meeting in a browser tab all work the same way. It never needs to detect which one you’re using.

Does it keep recordings?

No. Audio is turned into text on your Mac and never written to disk. What’s kept is the transcript, the answers and the notes, all on your Mac. Audio only leaves the Mac if you choose cloud recognition and agree to it.

Where do the answers come from? What account do I need?

From the answer engine you connect. With a ChatGPT account you can use Codex; otherwise, add an API key for any OpenAI-compatible service, such as DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi or OpenRouter, or use Ollama or LM Studio locally.

Will lots of materials slow the answers down?

It doesn’t stuff every file into the prompt. Materials are converted to structured text on your Mac, and each answer pulls only the passages relevant to the question, with the file and page they came from.

Is there an English interface?

Yes. Switch in Settings → Basics → Language and the app reopens in English; a few older advanced settings pages are still in Chinese for now. Suggested answers follow the language of the conversation, so an English interview gets English answers.

Do I have to re-allow screen recording after every update?

macOS ties those permissions to the app’s signature. Bind a local signature once in Settings → Basics, then update from inside the app and you won’t be asked again.

Does it run on an Intel Mac or on Windows?

No. It needs a Mac with Apple Silicon running macOS 14 or later.
